description: Every GitHub Actions workflow run of the NumPy repository created on 10 November 2026 (GitHub REST API, five pages of 100, no key). Queueing idea: Little's law, L = λW. The average number of items in a system equals their arrival rate times the average time each spends in it, whatever the arrival pattern, the service-time distribution or the scheduling, as long as the window is long compared with the time in the system. The steps turn each run into an interval (start → last update, Polars), count the runs in flight every minute L(t) on a 48-hour clock, compare the day's time-averaged L with λ·W, repeat it hour by hour, and split L into each workflow's λᵢWᵢ. The aha: the two sides are the same run-minutes counted two ways (the area under L(t), and the sum of the bars), so the law is bookkeeping, not a model; and because L adds up over parts, the workflows that hold the runners are the slow ones, not the frequent ones. Caveats: GitHub gives no end time per run, so the run's last update stands for it, and re-runs (which move a run's start) and runs updated more than 6 hours after starting are left out (the clean step marks them suspect); runs created the evening before and still running after midnight are missing, so early hours read low; a run holds several jobs, so this is load in runs, not in runners. Change created= in the queries (and owner/repo in the path) for another day or project; anonymous GitHub API calls are limited to 60 an hour.
name: Little's law in NumPy's CI
